title: Asphalt Sealcoating Explained: Reseal Every 2 to 4 Years
description: A residential asphalt sealcoat lasts about 2 to 4 years and shields sound pavement from sun and water; it will not fix potholes or cracks wider than 1/8 inch.
dek: A residential asphalt sealcoat lasts about 2 to 4 years and shields sound pavement from sun and water; it will not fix potholes or cracks wider than 1/8 inch.
intro: Sealcoating is a thin protective layer, usually an asphalt or coal tar emulsion loaded with fillers, spread over asphalt pavement to block sunlight, water and chemicals. It does not add strength, fill potholes or fix a failing base. On a sound driveway, resealed every two to four years, it can meaningfully slow the drying, graying and cracking that shorten asphalt's life. On a driveway that is already breaking up, it is cosmetic, and the money is better spent on repair.

quickAnswer: Sealcoating is cheap insurance for sound asphalt and wasted money on failing asphalt. Here is how to tell the difference, what goes into a proper job, and whether to do it yourself.

sections.h: What Sealcoating Is, and What It Is Not

blocks.p: Asphalt pavement is stone aggregate glued together with asphalt binder, a heavy petroleum product. The binder is what keeps the surface flexible and waterproof, and it is also what sunlight and oxygen attack. Over a few years the binder at the surface oxidizes, turns brittle and gray, and starts letting go of the fine aggregate. Sealcoating puts a sacrificial layer over that surface so the weather wears out the coating instead of the pavement.

In practice, sealcoat and driveway sealer are the same family of product. Contractors tend to say sealcoating and apply it from bulk tanks with spray rigs or squeegee machines; homeowners say sealing and apply it from pails with a squeegee. The chemistry overlaps heavily, although commercial material is often mixed with extra sand and polymer on site.

What sealcoating is not matters just as much. It is not an overlay, which is a new layer of hot asphalt, typically an inch and a half or more thick. It is not resurfacing, and it is not a structural repair. It will not fill potholes, level sunken areas or bind together asphalt that has broken into a web of cracks. A sealcoat over those problems hides them briefly and then fails along with the pavement.

Think of it like paint on a wood fence. Paint on sound boards adds years of life. Paint on rotten boards makes them look better until the next storm. The same judgment applies to asphalt, and it is the first decision in any sealcoating project.

Ultraviolet light and oxidation are the main targets. Fresh asphalt is black and slightly flexible; after a few summers of sun it fades to gray and becomes stiff. A dark sealcoat absorbs and blocks that sunlight, and it slows the oxygen reaction that hardens the binder. That is the main reason sealed driveways stay black and flexible longer.

Water intrusion is the second. Oxidized asphalt develops fine surface cracks and open texture, and water seeps into them. In cold climates that water freezes, expands and widens the cracks; in any climate it can reach the gravel base and soften it. A sealcoat with filler closes the finest openings and sheds rainwater. Larger cracks must be filled separately, since no sealcoat can bridge them.

Chemical resistance is the third. Gasoline, motor oil and transmission fluid dissolve asphalt binder, which is why oil stains often turn soft and crumbly over time. Sealcoats, especially those labeled fuel-resistant, slow that damage and make spills easier to clean. They do not make the surface fuel-proof, so prompt cleanup still matters.

Appearance is the visible benefit. A fresh, even black surface improves curb appeal and makes painted lines and edges look crisp. That is not a trivial benefit when you are selling a house, but it should be the bonus rather than the reason. Done only for looks on failing pavement, it rarely pays back.

sections.h: The Materials: Asphalt Emulsion, Coal Tar and Acrylic

blocks.p: Asphalt emulsion is the most common sealcoat for homes. It is asphalt binder dispersed in water with clay and emulsifiers, usually with mineral filler and often with polymers or latex for flexibility. It is compatible with asphalt pavement, relatively low in odor, cleans up with water while wet, and is what most pail sealers at the home center are. Our [ranked list of asphalt driveway sealers](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) covers the best of them.

Refined coal tar emulsion was long the commercial standard because it resists fuel and weathering very well. It is also much higher in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons than asphalt-based products. U.S. Geological Survey research tied coal-tar sealcoat to elevated PAH levels in house dust and nearby waterways, and several states, including Minnesota and Washington, plus many local governments, have banned or restricted it. For a home driveway, asphalt-based sealcoat is the responsible choice.

Acrylic and specialty polymer sealers sit at the premium end. They are non-asphalt coatings that can be pigmented, resist fuel well and stay flexible, but they cost considerably more and are used mainly on commercial lots, sports surfaces and decorative pavement. Few homeowners need them.

blocks.p: Oil-based or solvent-based rejuvenators are a separate category that soaks into old asphalt rather than coating it. They are used on badly oxidized pavement as a treatment, not as a routine sealcoat. Our [oil-based versus water-based sealer comparison](/oil-based-vs-water-based-driveway-sealer/) explains where they fit.

sections.h: How a Proper Sealcoating Job Goes

blocks.p: Preparation decides the result. A proper job starts by edging back grass and weeds, then thoroughly cleaning the surface with brooms, blowers and, where needed, a pressure washer. Any dirt, dust or vegetation left on the surface is where the sealcoat will bond, and it will lift with it.

Next, oil and fuel stains are scrubbed and treated with an oil-spot primer so the sealcoat can bond to them. Cracks are cleaned out and filled, usually with hot-pour rubberized filler on professional jobs or rope and pourable fillers on DIY ones. Small potholes and broken edges are patched. All of that needs to cure before the topcoat goes on. Our [crack filler guide](/best-driveway-crack-filler/) covers the DIY options.

The sealcoat is mixed thoroughly, because fillers settle, and applied in two thin coats. Contractors spray it or spread it with squeegee machines; homeowners pour and spread with a squeegee or brush. Edges and areas against the garage and walkways are cut in by hand. The second coat goes on only after the first is dry, often at a right angle for even coverage.

Then comes curing. The surface needs warmth and dry weather to cure, and cars should stay off for at least a day, often two. Barriers at the driveway entrance keep delivery drivers and visitors from rolling through it. Our guide on [driveway sealer drying times](/how-long-for-driveway-sealer-to-dry/) explains how weather affects this.

If a contractor skips the cleaning or crack filling, or applies only one coat to save time, the job will look good for a few months and fail early. Those steps are where the value is, and they are what you are paying for. Our [driveway sealing walkthrough](/how-to-seal-a-driveway/) covers the DIY version step by step.

sections.h: When to Sealcoat and How Often

blocks.p: New asphalt should not be sealcoated right away. Fresh pavement contains light oils that need time to evaporate, and sealing too early traps them, which can leave the surface soft. The common guidance is to wait at least six months and often up to a year, depending on climate and season of paving. See our article on [when to seal a new asphalt driveway](/when-should-you-seal-a-new-asphalt-driveway/) for the details.

After that, most residential driveways benefit from resealing every two to four years. Heavy traffic, full sun, hard winters and frequent oil drips push toward the shorter end; light traffic and shade push toward the longer. Sealing every year is usually overkill and can build up a thick layer that cracks and peels on its own.

The right time of year is a stretch of warm, dry days. Most sealcoat products need air and surface temperatures of about 50 degrees Fahrenheit and rising, with no rain for at least a day. Late spring through early fall is the typical window in most regions; very hot afternoons can make the sealcoat dry too fast and streak.

A practical way to judge timing is to look at the surface. When the black has faded to gray, the texture is opening up and water no longer beads, it is due. Our guide on [how often to seal your driveway](/how-often-should-you-seal-your-driveway/) covers the signs in more detail.

sections.h: Doing It Yourself or Hiring a Crew

blocks.p: DIY sealcoating is very doable on most residential driveways. It takes a weekend: one day for cleaning and crack filling and one for sealing. The tools are inexpensive, and pail sealers from home centers perform well when applied correctly. For a one- or two-car driveway, DIY usually saves a substantial share of a contractor's price.

Contractors bring commercial equipment and bulk material. Spray rigs lay down a more uniform coat quickly, hot-pour crack filler lasts longer than most DIY options, and commercial sealcoat is often mixed with sand for added texture and traction. For long, large or steep driveways, a crew can deliver a better result and save you a lot of physical work.
VET THE CREW
Ask five questions before you hire.

What product will you use, and is it coal-tar-free? Is crack filling included, and with what? Will you prime oil stains? How many coats? What is the cure time and who sets up barriers? Get the answers in writing on the quote.

Be cautious with door-to-door offers, particularly crews that say they have leftover material from a nearby job and can do yours cheaply today. That pitch is common in driveway scams, and the result is often a thin, watered-down coat or payment taken for work never finished. Use a local, established company with reviews and an address.

If you go DIY, our store guides for [Home Depot](/driveway-sealer-home-depot/) and [Menards](/driveway-sealer-menards/) list the pails worth buying, and our [Latex-ite review](/latex-ite-driveway-sealer-review/) covers one of the most common mid-range options in detail.

sections.h: What Sealcoating Costs and What It Is Worth

blocks.p: Professional residential sealcoating is commonly priced per square foot, often somewhere in the range of roughly 20 to 40 cents for a basic two-coat job, with crack filling, oil-spot treatment and patching added on. Many contractors also have a minimum job charge. For a typical two-car driveway, that often puts the total in the low to mid hundreds of dollars at the time of writing, varying by region.

DIY material costs vary with the product tier. Budget emulsions are inexpensive per pail; filler and polymer-modified sealers cost more but cover less area. For a two-car driveway with two coats, materials and basic tools usually come in below a contractor's price, but the gap narrows on large driveways.

blocks.p: The value of sealcoating lies in delaying the much larger cost of an overlay or replacement. Asphalt driveways commonly last somewhere around 15 to 25 years depending on climate, construction and care, and regular sealcoating and crack filling are the main things a homeowner can do to push toward the long end. Our breakdown of [sealing costs](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/) lays out the numbers in more detail.
Our [pros and cons of sealing asphalt](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/) article takes a balanced look at whether the investment pays back on your driveway.

sections.h: When Sealcoating Is a Waste of Money

blocks.p: Skip sealcoating, or at least do repairs first, if the driveway has alligator cracking, a network of interconnected cracks that looks like reptile skin. That pattern means the base underneath has failed, and the surface is moving under load. Sealcoat will crack along the same lines within months.

The same goes for potholes, sunken areas, ruts, and edges breaking off into the lawn. Those are structural problems that need patching, base repair, an overlay or full replacement. Spending money on sealcoat first only means paying for it twice.

Also skip it on freshly paved asphalt, as noted above, and in weather that will not let it cure. A sealcoat applied into cold nights or before a storm is money washed down the drain, sometimes literally.

Finally, do not sealcoat simply because a crew knocked on your door. If your driveway is still dark, tight and sheds water, it does not need another coat yet. Waiting a season costs nothing, while unnecessary coats build up and eventually crack and peel. For a full list of product options when the time does come, see our [best asphalt sealer picks](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/).

mistakes: Sealcoat is a protective skin, not a patch. Applying it over alligator cracks, potholes or broken edges hides them for a few weeks, then the same cracks reappear and the money is gone. Fix structural problems first, or accept that the driveway needs an overlay or replacement instead of a coating.
Sealing new asphalt in its first months

Fresh asphalt still contains light oils that must evaporate. Sealing too early traps them, which can leave the surface soft and prone to scuffing. Wait at least six months and often up to a year after paving, depending on climate, before the first coat goes on.

Frequent recoats build up a thick layer that becomes brittle, cracks on its own and starts to peel in flakes. Unless traffic is very heavy, a two to four year cycle is enough. Reseal when the surface looks gray and open, not on a calendar.
Hiring the crew with leftover material

Door-to-door offers of cheap sealcoat from a job down the street are a common setup for watered-down material or unfinished work. Hire an established local company, get the product and the process in writing, and never pay the full amount before the work is done.

One coat looks fine on day one, but it wears through in tire paths and turning areas within a season. Two thin coats, the second applied once the first has dried, give a far more durable result for little extra material and a few more hours of work.
bottomLine: Asphalt sealcoating is one of the best-value maintenance jobs around a house, as long as the pavement underneath is sound. It slows the oxidation, water intrusion and chemical damage that shorten asphalt's life, keeps the surface looking dark and clean, and costs a small fraction of an overlay or replacement. Use an asphalt-based product, fill cracks first, apply two thin coats in warm weather and reseal every two to four years. Where the driveway is already failing, put the money into repair instead. And whether you do it yourself or hire a crew, the work that happens before the sealcoat goes on, cleaning, crack filling and oil treatment, decides how long the result lasts.

faqs.q: Is sealcoating the same thing as sealing a driveway?
faqs.a: Essentially yes. Both put a protective coat of asphalt emulsion or a similar material over the pavement. Sealcoating is the term contractors usually use for bulk-applied commercial material, often sprayed and mixed with sand. Sealing is the homeowner term for pail products applied with a squeegee. The purpose and the prep are the same.

faqs.q: How long does a sealcoat last on a residential driveway?
faqs.a: Most residential sealcoats last about two to four years before the surface looks faded and needs another coat. Heavy traffic, full sun, freeze-thaw climates and oil drips shorten that; light traffic and shade extend it. Tire paths and turning areas wear first, so a partial touch-up can sometimes stretch the cycle.

faqs.q: Can sealcoat fill cracks in my driveway?
faqs.a: Only the finest hairline cracks. Filler sealers can bridge very narrow surface checking, but any crack wider than roughly an eighth of an inch needs a dedicated crack filler first, allowed to cure before the sealcoat goes on. Sealcoat poured into open cracks shrinks and splits, and water keeps reaching the base.

faqs.q: How soon can I drive on a freshly sealcoated driveway?
faqs.a: Usually after 24 to 48 hours in warm, dry weather, and longer in cool, humid or shaded conditions. Walking is often fine after several hours. Avoid turning the steering wheel while parked on a fresh coat, since it scuffs the surface. Block the entrance with tape or cones so nobody drives on it early.

faqs.q: Does sealcoating add value to a home?
faqs.a: It improves curb appeal, which can help a house show better, and regular sealing extends the life of the driveway, delaying the cost of replacement. It is unlikely to add measurable appraisal value on its own. Think of it as maintenance that protects the value already there, not as an upgrade.

faqs.q: Is coal tar sealcoat still used?
faqs.a: It is still made and used in some areas, but several states, including Minnesota and Washington, and many local governments have banned or restricted it because of its high PAH content. Asphalt-based sealcoats are widely available, perform well, and are the safer choice for homes. Ask any contractor in writing what product they use.

faqs.q: What temperature is too cold to sealcoat?
faqs.a: Most asphalt emulsion sealcoats require air and surface temperatures of at least about 50 degrees Fahrenheit and rising, with nights that stay reasonably mild. Below that, the water in the emulsion evaporates too slowly and the coat may not cure before it is damaged by dew, rain or traffic. Very hot surfaces can also cause problems.
